fields.h1: Build a Sermon Evaluation Form Preachers Learn From
fields.hero_description: Build a sermon evaluation form listeners fill in on a phone, with each area averaged into one summary for the preacher.
fields.features_heading: What a Stack of Sermon Sheets Leaves Out
fields.features_subheading: Paper feedback waits in a folder until someone types it up. Emergent builds the form and the app that adds the scores.
fields.feature_1:
Four areas scored on one 1 to 5 scale

Each listener rates the handling of the text, the main idea, the application, and the delivery from 1 to 5. Using one scale for all four lets the preacher compare them directly.
fields.feature_2:
A comment attached to every low score

A score of 2 or lower asks the listener what was missing before they can move on. The note stays with that area, so the reason sits right next to the number it explains.
fields.feature_3:
Averages across every listener

The app averages each area across everyone who filled in the form that week. The preacher sees application at 2.8 and the main idea at 4.4 instead of reading five sheets.
fields.feature_4:
One summary in the preacher's inbox

When the last form is in, the preacher gets one email with each area's average and every comment. Names can stay off the summary when the team wants its feedback anonymous.
fields.feature_5:
Scores tracked across a sermon series

Every response is saved by date and sermon title in a database the church owns. A chart plots each area's average week by week, so a change in delivery shows up in the scores.
fields.feature_6:
Code that moves with the church

On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and host the form next to the church's other tools. Keep building on it by prompting Emergent or by editing the code.

fields.tab_content_1:
Application trails at 2.8 when all five scores are in

Five volunteers sit in different rows at Calloway Creek Church. By Monday noon, each one scores the sermon 1 to 5 in four areas, and the app averages the five. This week the main idea averaged 4.4 and application came in at 2.8, with 3 comments asking for a concrete step to take.
fields.tab_content_2:
In the preaching lab, the professor's scores stay separate

Abbington Seminary holds its preaching lab on Thursdays. Nine classmates and Professor Loftis score each student sermon on the same form. After Hannah Penner preached on Jonah 4, the class averaged 3.6 on the main idea and the professor gave it a 3. The app shows faculty scores in a column of their own.
fields.tab_content_3:
Three candidates, one form, averages side by side

Seven members of the Glenhollow Fellowship search committee watched one recorded sermon from each of 3 candidates and scored all three on the same form at home. The app lines up each candidate's averages by area. Candidate B leads on handling the text at 4.6, and Candidate A leads on delivery at 4.3.
fields.tab_content_4:
Each Sunday's clarity score, charted for 10 weeks

Pastor Gil Garland wanted to know whether his main point was landing. Harvest Lane Church scored all 10 sermons of a Philippians series on the same form, including whether the main idea was clear. In week 4 he began stating the point in a single sentence. That score averaged 3.1 in week 1 and 4.2 in week 10.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Sermon Evaluation Form
fields.howto_description: Follow these seven steps to set up a sermon evaluation form that hands the preacher area scores and comments each week.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide who will listen for you
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Choose the areas you want scored
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Score every area on the same scale
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Ask for a reason behind low scores
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick three to six people who hear the sermon from different seats: a longtime member, a newer attender, a high school student. Ask each one to commit for a full quarter. Scores from the same listeners are easier to compare week to week.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Keep the form to four or five areas a listener can judge after one hearing: how the text was handled, whether the main idea came through, how the application landed, and how the delivery came across. Add an area only when you plan to act on it.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Use 1 to 5 for every area, with a short label at each end of the scale. One shared scale lets the app average across listeners and compare areas with each other. Mixing stars, yes or no, and 1 to 10 makes the summary hard to read.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Show a comment box whenever a listener gives a 2 or lower, and keep it optional above that. The comment tells the preacher what to change, which a bare number cannot do. Ask for one sentence rather than a paragraph.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Set a deadline for every response
fields.howto_step_5_des: Close the form at a fixed time, such as Monday noon, while the sermon is still fresh in memory. When it closes, the preacher gets a single summary of the averages and comments instead of a trickle of separate replies.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Some teams attach names so the preacher can follow up with a listener; others hide them. Choose before the first Sunday and state the choice at the top of the form. Listeners then know exactly who will read their comments.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Build it, then review the first month
fields.howto_step_7_des: Describe the areas, the scale, the deadline, and the summary to Emergent, and it builds the form, the database, and the averages. After four Sundays, check which areas actually move and drop any question that gets rushed answers.
